body.p: Remarks
Independent Claims

In the instant Summary, Applicant has explained that "while the game engine may be used to generate multiple video streams, i.e., one from the player character viewpoint and others from the viewpoints of NPCs, as recognized herein, this can be computationally expensive." Applicant then explains that a single video can be transformed using ML "to avoid rendering multiple viewpoints simultaneously".

Ye does precisely what Applicant, and the instant claims, avoid. As will be demonstrated in detail, Ye uses ML merely to select which of plural pre-existing camera views (i.e., video streams) to present to a person.

Claim 1 expresses a solution to the problem identified in the Summary in the following manner: among other limitations, a first screen render from a player character (PC) viewpoint is presented to at least one ML model and a transform of that render is received back from the model, with the transform being a NPC viewpoint. Note that Claim 1 expressly requires the ML model to return the transformed render itself, not merely identify which one of multiple preexisting renders to use.

Claim 8 expresses present principles by reciting inputting to a ML model a PC video stream and receiving back from the ML model a NPC video stream for the computer simulation, among other limitations. Along these lines, among other limitations Claim 15 requires generating, using computer simulation video techniques, a first video from a viewpoint of a first character controllable by a player,
inputting that video into a ML model, and receiving from the ML model at least a second video from a viewpoint of a second character not controllable by a player.

Now let's turn to Ye and the rejection's reliance in most relevant part primarily on paragraphs 65 and 72-76. In paragraph 16, Ye expressly teaches doing what the instant summary seeks to avoid: re-executing the video game to generate the active spectator camera view.

In paragraph 51, Ye states that "A view recommendation engine executing at the game cloud site 300 is used to identify and provide the specific camera views to the passive spectator. The view recommendation engine uses a recommendation model to identify specific ones of camera views of the video game for returning to the passive spectator." Thus, paragraph 51 assumes preexisting camera views; nowhere does paragraph 51 assert any transform of a view being received from the ML model, but only an identification of which one of the preexisting view to select.

In paragraph 52, Ye reiterates that "Frames of the specific ones of the camera views identified for the passive spectator are forwarded to a game engine for processing, encoding and streaming to the client device of the passive spectator, where the streams are decoded and rendered." Paragraph 56 divulges that figure 2A of Ye shows the generation of multiple camera views.

Paragraph 65 of Ye, cited in the Office Action, explicitly states that "the view recommendation engine also receives the various camera views generatedfrom game play data 308 of game 1" and that the output of the recommendation engine "is used "to select [not transform] specific one of the camera views."
Paragraph 72 of Ye further makes Applicant's case: "The feature processing engine 401 extracts the image data 311 from the image datastore 311 and processes the image data 311 to extract

various features of the images captured in each camera view of game play data". The ensuing paragraphs of Ye teach that these features are input to the recommendation engine along with spectator characteristics and preferences to enable the engine to "identif[y] the camera views to be provided to the passive spectator", e.g., paragraph 73.

Accordingly, because Ye fails to teach a ML model that does not merely identify a preexisting camera view but instead returns a transform of an input render (Claim 1), the rejection should be withdrawn. Claims 8 and 15 likewise are patentable over Ye, mutatis mutandis.
Claims 4, 13, and 19

These claims explicitly require a single viewpoint to be rendered, and then using a ML model for transforming the single viewpoint to output video at viewpoints of one or more other NPCs in the area in a single inference pass. The rejection cites paragraphs 65 and 72 of Ye but as demonstrated above, these paragraphs envision selecting one of multiple preexisting renders.
Claims 5, 14, and 20

These claims require the first screen render to be sent from a cloud server to at least one display for presentation of the first screen render at a first time and actions of NPCs to be delayed for at least one frame while the ML model generates the second screen render. The rejection cites paragraphs 49, 16, and 54 (in the order listed in the Office Action) but these paragraphs do not say what the examiner alleges they say. Paragraph 16 of Ye teaches nothing more relevant than re-executing the video game to generate the active spectator camera view. Paragraph 49 teaches nothing more relevant than a video

game being executed locally at client devices and metadata from the executing video game being transmitted to a game cloud server. Paragraph 54 merely states at its most relevant that a game engine manages the game logic of the game, collects and transmits inputs to the game logic, and manages the allocation and synchronization of the functional portions of the game engine to render the game. Nowhere in this relied-upon subject matter is there any mention of sending a first screen render from a cloud server for presentation of the first screen render at a first time while delaying actions of NPCs for at least one frame while the ML model generates the second screen render. Nothing of the sort appears in the relied-upon subject matter.
